payload.rationale: No current data were supplied, so this rests on background knowledge through roughly early 2026. Observed facts: US measles cases in 2025 reached roughly 2,200+, the highest since 1992, driven by the West Texas outbreak that peaked in Feb–April and faded by summer. Entering 2026, large outbreaks were active in South Carolina (Upstate, several hundred to ~900+ cases) and Utah/Arizona, and the national 2026 count was already in the high hundreds within the first ~two months, a materially faster pace than 2025. Transfer assumptions: measles in the US remains outbreak-driven with strong late-winter/spring seasonality; sustaining >6,000 cases in a calendar year would require either multiple large concurrent outbreaks continuing through summer/fall or a fall resurgence, which would be historically unusual since elimination but not implausible given declining MMR coverage and possible loss of elimination status. A plausible central expectation for 2026 is roughly 2,500–5,000 cases, with a meaningful right tail. Too high risk: if the early-2026 outbreaks were largely contained by late spring (as in 2025), the final tally may land well under 6,000, and by September the trajectory could already make YES nearly impossible. Too low risk: the early-2026 pace was well above 2025's, undervaccinated communities are widespread, and importations from Canada/Mexico were high; if transmission stayed elevated through the summer, 6,000+ becomes likely, and I lack the actual mid-2026 CDC counts that would sharply resolve this. Also note resolution uses the CDC figure as of expiration without later revisions, which slightly favors NO due to reporting lag.
limitations: No supplied evidence; no knowledge of actual CDC counts between roughly early 2026 and the September 2026 cutoff.
Seasonality and outbreak-containment assumptions are drawn from 2025 and prior years and may not hold in 2026.
CDC reporting lag and the no-revisions rule could affect the settlement figure relative to true incidence.
